The closest direct precedent is [MTAM, CIKM 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.08598): temporal gates modify recurrent state transitions and information filtering; its time-aware GRU captures short-term intent. [TLSRec, CIKM 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.04760) uses a neural time gate to regulate long- versus short-term preference contributions per embedding dimension. These support adaptive temporal retention, but do not establish that hard hidden-state resets outperform learned forgetting or recency-weighted BPR-max.

Recent evidence supports modeling irregular gaps, with limited direct evidence for GRU resets. [TiCoSeRec, AAAI 2023](https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/view/25540) links uneven interaction intervals to preference drift and proposes time-aware augmentation. [GRUT, EMNLP 2025](https://aclanthology.org/2025.findings-emnlp.1300.pdf) models timestamps and intervals in generative recommendation; its architecture and trend-based inference do not directly transfer to the required GRU4Rec experiment. The retrieved literature did not establish a 2023–2026 GRU reset method validated under the specified Amazon protocol.

Experiment hypothesis, inferred from these findings: retain one jointly trained GRU per category and learn a dimension-wise retention gate from log-scaled observed inter-event gaps, previous hidden state, and current item embedding; attenuate the previous state before the GRU update. Compare against unchanged recency-weighted BPR-max, then ablate gap-only decay versus content-conditioned forgetting under identical seeds, budgets, and macro validation HR@10. Use only gaps between observed history events; the next interaction’s timestamp is unavailable at prediction. Treat benefits as unproven until measured, and preserve useful persistent preferences rather than assuming every long gap signals an intent reset.
